facts.claim: "Hope" is a song by American rapper NF. It was released on February 16, 2023, as the lead single from his fifth studio album, also called Hope.
NF wrote the song with Tommee Profitt. The two produced it with Jeff Sojka.
The official music video came out the same day as the song. NF and Patrick Tohill directed it.
The song opens with plucky piano chords. These move into staccato strings and a pulsing echo of background voices.

The song is the opening track on the album Hope. One reviewer says it marks a turning point in which NF accepts change and lets go of his pride. The same review says the lighter side of NF takes control in the last line, "I'm taking the reins."
In the video, NF plays two versions of himself. One wears all white and wants to change and find hope. The other wears all black and wants to stay the same.
Lyrically, NF speaks to his former self after about 30 years of struggle. He says he is done waiting on false promises and is moving forward in hope.
The Hope album was preceded by the singles "Hope" and "Motto". A third single, "Happy", came out the same day as the album.
Hope debuted at number two on the US Billboard 200 with 123,000 album-equivalent units. This was NF's third top-ten album.
NF told NME that making the album felt harder than before. He said the pressure was greater than ever because so long had passed since his last album.

research.lineage: NF's Hope sits in the confessional, mental-health-focused rap tradition. It pairs rapid, slam-poetry-style lyrics with cinematic orchestral production from longtime collaborator Tommee Profitt, and critics often compare it to Eminem's style.

draft:
**HOPE** begins with a firing. NF turns to the person who has run things for three decades, the one "draggin' your feet" and blaming everyone else for the standstill, and tells him his time is up. That person is NF. The address is warm and merciless at once: "Nate, you've had a great run." It's the tone of a boss letting down a loyal employee, and the kindness makes it sting more. Then, like an emcee clearing the stage, the song introduces its own album. That fits, since "Hope" is the opening track and the lead single of the record named after it.

What follows is a definition of success in a rapid, list-like build, the slam-poetry cadence critics have long tied to Eminem. Taking a pay cut to do what you love. Turning failure into fuel. Then the song stops reciting and starts confessing. NF calls a mental breakdown "the push I needed" to get help, and admits it took becoming a father to look in the mirror. The most tender moment is also the most tangled. Picking up a son each morning, NF promises the boy will never stand at a window wondering if dad will come home, then turns to a parent: "Mama, I forgive you." Forgiveness and old injury sit in the same line, and the song doesn't pretend one cancels the other. The fear underneath isn't for NF at all. It's that a child might grow up feeling never enough.

The craft shows in the long "30 years of" litany, more than thirty rounds of the same phrase with a new word stapled on each time: hollow, bitter, stagnant, lonely. The repetition is the point. Shame feels like a sentence you keep serving, and the list keeps going until it lands on "pushing everyone away." Then the old self breaks in, in parentheses, telling the new one "you'll never be loved." The current voice answers each charge until the last line, where the doubting voice cuts in with "(no)" and the claim to take the reins has to be made twice before it sticks.

Tommee Profitt, NF's longtime collaborator, co-wrote and co-produced it with NF and Jeff Sojka, carrying their cinematic orchestral approach: plucky piano chords giving way to staccato strings and a pulsing echo of background voices. In the video, which NF co-directed with Patrick Tohill, the split is literal, one NF in white reaching for change, one in black wanting to stay put. NF told NME the pressure on this album was greater than ever after so long away. The song turns that weight into an argument with the mirror.

It sticks because you hear someone win an argument with the worst voice in their own head by one interrupted word, and you know exactly how close it was.

factCheck.claim: The song begins with a firing.
factCheck.note: The lyrics open with 'Hope / I'm on my way, I'm coming' before the 30-years address. Reworded to 'turns on a firing' so it makes no claim about how the song starts.

factCheck.claim: The addressee is 'draggin' your feet' and blaming everyone else for the standstill.
factCheck.note: The quote is exact. The lyric is 'Tellin' me I'm the reason we're stagnant', so the addressee pins the standstill on the narrator, not on everyone else. Fixed.

factCheck.claim: The person addressed is NF himself.
factCheck.note: Plugged In: NF speaks to his former self after about 30 years of struggle. The lyric also says 'Nate'.

factCheck.claim: "Nate, you've had a great run."
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly.

factCheck.claim: The song introduces its own album; 'Hope' is the opening track and lead single of the album Hope.
factCheck.note: The lyrics ('I'd like to introduce my... album... HOPE') and the facts agree.

factCheck.claim: The slam-poetry cadence critics have long tied to Eminem.
factCheck.note: The packet says critics 'often compare' it to Eminem. 'Long tied' overstated the history. Fixed.

factCheck.claim: Taking a pay cut to do what you love; turning failure into fuel.
factCheck.note: Matches 'take the pay cut' and 'turn 'em into motivation'.

factCheck.claim: NF calls a mental breakdown "the push I needed" to get help.
factCheck.note: Exact lyric fragment, and the context is in the lyrics.

factCheck.claim: Picking up a son each morning; promises he won't wonder if dad will come home.
factCheck.note: The lyrics say 'every day' and 'show up', not 'each morning' and 'come home'. Fixed.

factCheck.claim: "Mama, I forgive you."
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics.

factCheck.claim: The fear is that a child might grow up feeling never enough.

factCheck.claim: More than thirty rounds of '30 years of' with words like hollow, bitter, stagnant, lonely, ending on 'pushing everyone away'.
factCheck.note: The lyrics have 32 instances. All the words and the quote are present.

factCheck.claim: The old self breaks in in parentheses with 'you'll never be loved'.
factCheck.note: Matches '(You'll never be loved, you'll never be safe)'. Reading it as the old self fits the facts.

factCheck.claim: The doubting voice cuts in with '(no)' and the claim to take the reins is made twice.
factCheck.note: Lyrics: 'I'm taking the- (no)' then 'I'm taking the / Reins'. 'Last line' loosened to 'closing lines'.
